extracted.intended_audience: indie audio drama creators, fiction podcasters, audio storytellers, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating memorable, original audio dramas by using setting, sound design, genre-mixing, and concrete detail to avoid repetitive 'space station' tropes and setting fatigue. Focuses on world-building, format choices, and creative habits that broaden distinctiveness in fiction podcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being 'another' space show (originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: "You never want to be another space show." Don’t default to copying a successful property (e.g., Wolf 359) so your show doesn’t read as interchangeable with dozens of similar podcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: marketing blurbs and synopses that are basically 'like Wolf 359 but...'. If a show feels so interchangeable that the crucial differences are 'deeply hidden in the text', it may not be worth listeners' time. Aim for a distinct identity rather than reusing the same premise/brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to give the show a distinct identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting should provide the show's 'meat on its bones' and a distinct identity that traces back to varied inspirations rather than generic backdrop noise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example prompts: 'How would a hospital in space sound and operate?' (EOS 10), or 'a sci-fi take on The Devil Wears Prada' (Inkwrym). Use setting-driven questions to inform character, plot, tone and sound design so the location feels integral, not incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break setting redundancy by choosing non-space locales
rubrics_metrics.description: To combat sci‑fi surplus, consider settings outside of spacecraft/space stations — sprawling cities, childhood homes, suburbs, malls, grocery stores, coffee shops, restaurants, the sea, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete suggestion list offered as alternatives; these different everyday or unexpected locations offer unique assets for music, sound design, and atmosphere. Anti-pattern: defaulting to 'exclusively inside a spacecraft' because it flattens variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stock sensory/sci-fi clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and limit overused 'go‑tos' that make many space shows feel identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common cliché elements listed: rickety, somewhat out of date machinery; loudly clacking keyboards; handheld tape recorders as framing devices; small windows with starry horizons; baggy jumpsuits and lace-up boots; bad food made cozy by sentimentality. These aren’t always bad but become a problem when relied on reflexively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage setting for sound design and overall vibe
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting should directly inform the music, sound design, and general vibe of the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sonic choices to sell the environment (hospital beeps vs creaky ship engines, alien ambient textures, city soundscapes). The article emphasizes that world-building opportunities 'greatly impact the music, sound design, and general vibe.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ambitious, fearless, and willing to be niche
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not default to safe trends or focus-tested sameness; creatives should have the courage to be niche and esoteric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post urges making work 'with ambition, with a sort of fearlessness to be niche, esoteric even.' Anti-pattern: fearing creativity and becoming complacent with repetition and minor differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix genres and inspirations to produce distinct takes
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine disparate inspirations and genres to yield novel premises rather than adhering strictly to a single trope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: medical drama in space (EOS 10), fashion-industry sci-fi (Inkwrym), space road-trip comedy (StarTripper!!). Cited inspiration sources range from Farscape to My So-Called Life, showing how cross-genre influences contribute to originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete, micromanaged details to flesh out setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, specific sensory details make a setting feel lived-in and distinctive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'MTV era punk rock etched into its DNA,' 'coffee smell and underground subways' or a 'space trailer park.' The piece praises shows where 'every little detail feels micromanaged to fill out their audio Pinterest board.' These details let listeners' imaginations fill in the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore alternative formats: short-form, anthologies, experimental structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider non-linear, short-form, anthology, or experimental formats instead of only long serial narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised examples: THE INFINITE NOW (experimental short-form transmissions), anthology collections like Obsidian and PodCube, and short-form pieces such as Community Cat News. These formats can avoid tired tropes and offer freshness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft titles and summaries that communicate distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles and short descriptions are crucial filters for listeners and should indicate what truly sets a show apart rather than relying on generic buzzwords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author used titles/summaries to find shows; anti-pattern: synopses that read as checklist of buzzwords (e.g., 'dysfunctional crew in a spaceship') which makes discovery and evaluation harder. Strong, unusual loglines (e.g., 'Two Flat Earthers Kidnap a Freemason') signal originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consume widely across media to expand creative range
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad media consumption fosters a wider creative palette; creators should read/watch/listen outside their immediate niche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice quoted: 'Fiction authors should read nonfiction books, soap opera fans should play horror games...' Using a variety of media inputs helps avoid creative tunnel vision and produces more original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let inspirations inform but don’t let them dictate your output
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit and study influences but aim to synthesize them into something new rather than producing close imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Urbina credits Farscape and My So-Called Life as inspiration; the combination of different influences gives Wolf 359 its distinct identity. Use inspirations as raw material to create original combinations rather than templates to copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make memorable art over market‑safe art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize meaningful, memorable creative choices over following what seems guaranteed to attract broad audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author clarifies this is not an attack on making sci‑fi; it's a call to utilize the genre better and not to make art that merely adheres to perceived marketable tropes. Value projects that 'stand for everything that audio drama was deliberately built on' rather than safe replicas.
